On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability

Xiangdong Zhang    Xiaohan Qin    Sunan Zou    Tuo Dai    Bizhao Shi    Zhuo Xia    Yebin Yang    Yizhou Chen    Yuliang Liu    Yu Cheng    Junchi Yan Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4%\mathbf{2.4\%} extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.

1 Introduction

Residual connections support optimization and information propagation in modern language models (He et al., 2016a; He et al., 2016b; Vaswani et al., 2017; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b), and recent work improves language modeling and depth utilization by enriching this pathway (Pagliardini et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). Hyper-Connections (HC) (Zhu et al., 2025) introduce multiple residual streams with learned read, write, and mixing operations for flexible information routing. The manifold-constrained variant, mHC (Xie et al., 2025), constrains residual mixing to improve training stability at scale. HC-based architectures, particularly mHC, have been adopted in frontier language models (Xu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). Despite the growing adoption, these architectures remain insufficiently understood and costly to train: their gating and mixing operations introduce architectural complexity and non-negligible execution overhead, even under efficient implementations (Xie et al., 2025).

A key source of this overhead is repeated access to the expanded residual state: at every sublayer, HC-style mappings read and write nn streams of width CC to generate gates, aggregate inputs, and propagate updates. This memory traffic incurs costs not captured by FLOPs alone. In our end-to-end experiments with an efficient implementation, mHC adds 7%−27%7\%-27\% training time over a vanilla baseline (Figure 3(a)), despite adding less than 1%1\% FLOPs. This motivates reconsidering the underlying read, write, and mixing interactions. We ask: Can a simpler Hyper-Connections design reduce execution cost while preserving model quality and training stability at scale?

In this work, we systematically study the Hyper-Connections architecture through three components: read gates, write gates, and residual mixing. We find that unconstrained mixing improves quality, but Sinkhorn constraints substantially reduce its benefit. Learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates each achieve quality comparable to mHC, with further gains from combining them. Our analysis also highlights the propagation risks of unconstrained mixing, leading us to select learned read/write gating with identity transitions as a minimal effective structure that retains competitive quality while avoiding these risks.

Without residual mixing, the additive structure lets scalar corrections exactly recover preceding output contributions for given gates, without materializing intermediate n​CnC-dimensional states. Gate generation, however, still accesses the updated state at every sublayer. We reduce these accesses by computing layer-specific gates from a common group-entry state, consolidating reads and deferring writes across sublayers. We call this execution scheme shared memory access.

Together, these findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture through learned read/write gates without mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access. We also develop specialized kernels to translate this simplicity into training efficiency. As shown in Figure 1(a), SimpleHC incurs only 2.4%2.4\% additional training cost at the largest tested scale and halves memory traffic from 18​C18C to 9​C9C per sublayer relative to fused mHC. It achieves downstream performance comparable to mHC and identityHC on 15B and 30B MoE models (Figure 1(c)). Analyses in Section 6 further support the design of SimpleHC. It also exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during training and remains stable under stress-test settings.

2 Preliminaries

Hyper-Connections (HC, dynamic variant) (Zhu et al., 2025) and Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) (Xie et al., 2025) share a multi-stream residual structure. The two methods differ in how their coefficients are conditioned and parameterized, and whether residual mixing is constrained.

Each Transformer block contains two sublayers: attention and FFN/MoE. Let Xl∈ℝn×CX_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times C} contain nn width-CC residual streams entering sublayer ll. All vectors are column vectors; vec⁡(Xl)∈ℝn​C×1\operatorname{vec}(X_{l})\in\mathbb{R}^{nC\times 1} concatenates streams in row order. We omit token and batch indices unless stated; II denotes the n×nn\times n identity matrix. Both methods compute ul=Xl⊤​hlpreu_{l}=X_{l}^{\top}h_{l}^{\mathrm{pre}}, ol=Fl​(ul)o_{l}=F_{l}(u_{l}), and Xl+1=Hlres​Xl+hlpost​ol⊤X_{l+1}=H_{l}^{\mathrm{res}}X_{l}+h_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}o_{l}^{\top}. The read and write gates hlpre,hlpost∈ℝn×1h_{l}^{\mathrm{pre}},h_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 1} aggregate stream states and distribute sublayer outputs; Hlres∈ℝn×nH_{l}^{\mathrm{res}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} mixes streams. Here, ul,ol∈ℝC×1u_{l},o_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times 1}, and FlF_{l} denotes the sublayer module.

HC projects each normalized CC-dimensional stream using Wlpre,Wlpost∈ℝC×1W_{l}^{\mathrm{pre}},W_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times 1} and Wlres∈ℝC×nW_{l}^{\mathrm{res}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times n}, shared across streams within each sublayer. Scaled tanh\tanh projections are added to learned static coefficients, yielding read/write gates and unconstrained residual mixing.

In contrast, mHC uses the normalized full state zl=RMSNorm⁡(vec⁡(Xl))∈ℝn​C×1z_{l}=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\operatorname{vec}(X_{l}))\in\mathbb{R}^{nC\times 1} to compute ℓls=αls​(Wls)⊤​zl+bls\ell_{l}^{s}=\alpha_{l}^{s}(W_{l}^{s})^{\top}z_{l}+b_{l}^{s} for s∈{pre,post,res}s\in\{\mathrm{pre},\mathrm{post},\mathrm{res}\}. Here, Wlpre,Wlpost∈ℝn​C×nW_{l}^{\mathrm{pre}},W_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}\in\mathbb{R}^{nC\times n} and Wlres∈ℝn​C×n2W_{l}^{\mathrm{res}}\in\mathbb{R}^{nC\times n^{2}}. Each αls\alpha_{l}^{s} is a learned scalar; logits and learned biases have nn entries for read/write gates and n2n^{2} for mixing. Parameters are independent across operations and sublayers. mHC applies sigmoid to read logits, twice sigmoid to write logits, and Sinkhorn normalization to mixing logits reshaped into an n×nn\times n matrix. Sinkhorn approximately enforces a doubly stochastic HlresH_{l}^{\mathrm{res}} to stabilize propagation across depth. Unless otherwise stated, we use the full-state gate parameterization of mHC.

3 SimpleHC

We propose SimpleHC, a Hyper-Connections architecture with a simplified residual structure and execution scheme (Figure 2). It retains multiple residual streams and learned read/write gates while removing residual mixing. Shared memory access reduces repeated state access by generating layer-specific gates from group-entry states, batching reads, and deferring writes.

3.1 Simplifying the Residual Structure

Prior work observed that removing residual mixing from mHC by setting Hlres=IH_{l}^{\mathrm{res}}=I (identityHC) largely preserves model quality (Guo et al., 2026). identityHC has also been adopted in Hy4 preview (Tencent Hy Team, 2026). Building on these insights, our systematic study reveals an important distinction: unconstrained residual mixing improves model quality, whereas Sinkhorn-constrained mixing offers little benefit over identity transitions (Table 2). The gains from unconstrained mixing, however, come with the risk of cumulative signal amplification or attenuation across depth (Section 6.1).

We therefore retain learned read/write gates with identity transitions as a minimal effective structure, preserving competitive quality while avoiding residual matrix products, with Xl+1=Xl+hlpost​ol⊤X_{l+1}=X_{l}+h_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}o_{l}^{\top}. With zl=RMSNorm⁡(vec⁡(Xl))z_{l}=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\operatorname{vec}(X_{l})) and ℓls=αls​(Wls)⊤​zl+bls\ell_{l}^{s}=\alpha_{l}^{s}(W_{l}^{s})^{\top}z_{l}+b_{l}^{s} for s∈{pre,post}s\in\{\mathrm{pre},\mathrm{post}\}, SimpleHC uses hlpre=σ⁡(ℓlpre)h_{l}^{\mathrm{pre}}=\sigma(\ell_{l}^{\mathrm{pre}}) and hlpost=2​σ​(ℓlpost)h_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}=2\sigma(\ell_{l}^{\mathrm{post}}). Without residual mixing, updates accumulate additively. Given the state XLX_{L} at sublayer LL, the residual state at any later sublayer jj is

Xj=XL+∑k=Lj−1hkpost​ok⊤.X_{j}=X_{L}+\sum_{k=L}^{j-1}h_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}o_{k}^{\top}. (1)

Each term adds a preceding sublayer’s output to the streams according to its write gate, and subsequent residual transitions leave this allocation unchanged.

3.2 Shared Memory Access

Even without residual mixing, conventional execution accesses the n​CnC-dimensional state at every sublayer to generate gates, form inputs, and write updates. We introduce shared memory access across sublayers to reduce this traffic. With additive updates, each preceding output contributes to a later input through the inner product of its write gate and the later read gate. Substituting Equation 1 into the read operation gives:

uj=Xj⊤​hjpre=XL⊤​hjpre+∑k=Lj−1((hjpre)⊤​hkpost)⏟scalar coefficient​ok.u_{j}=X_{j}^{\top}h_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}=X_{L}^{\top}h_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}+\sum_{k=L}^{j-1}\underbrace{\bigl((h_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}})^{\top}h_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}\bigr)}_{\text{scalar coefficient}}o_{k}. (2)

We call XL⊤​hjpreX_{L}^{\top}h_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}} the base read and the remaining terms scalar corrections, each weighting a preceding CC-dimensional output by a scalar coefficient. For given gates, this reconstructs the input without writing intermediate updates into the n​CnC-dimensional residual state.

This reconstruction assumes that the gates are already available. However, computing hjs=gjs​(Xj)h_{j}^{s}=g_{j}^{s}(X_{j}) requires materializing and accessing the updated state at every sublayer, where gjsg_{j}^{s} is the gate mapping defined above for s∈{pre,post}s\in\{\mathrm{pre},\mathrm{post}\}. SimpleHC relaxes this dependency by generating gates for KK consecutive sublayers from a common group-entry state XLX_{L}:

h¯jpre=gjpre​(XL),h¯jpost=gjpost​(XL),L≤j<L+K.\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}=g_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}(X_{L}),\qquad\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{post}}=g_{j}^{\mathrm{post}}(X_{L}),\qquad L\leq j<L+K. (3)

Within groups, sublayers retain independent gate parameters but share the conditioning state XLX_{L}. Relative to per-sublayer conditioning, the only approximation is generating gates from XLX_{L} rather than XjX_{j}. Grouped gate generation computes layer-specific gates jointly from XLX_{L}, reducing state reads from KK to 11 and making group gates available upfront. With these gates, Equation 2 becomes

uj=XL⊤​h¯jpre+∑k=Lj−1dj,k​ok,dj,k=(h¯jpre)⊤​h¯kpost.u_{j}=X_{L}^{\top}\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}+\sum_{k=L}^{j-1}d_{j,k}o_{k},\qquad d_{j,k}=(\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}})^{\top}\bar{h}_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}. (4)

All KK base reads are batched into one scan of XLX_{L}, with dj,kd_{j,k} precomputed at group entry. Corrections incorporate preceding CC-dimensional outputs without intermediate n​CnC-dimensional state writes.

Within each group, sublayers execute sequentially, passing each oj=Fj​(uj)o_{j}=F_{j}(u_{j}) to later inputs through scalar corrections. A single fused kernel writes back all updates at the group boundary:

XL+K=XL+∑k=LL+K−1h¯kpost​ok⊤.X_{L+K}=X_{L}+\sum_{k=L}^{L+K-1}\bar{h}_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}o_{k}^{\top}. (5)

This execution is algebraically equivalent to sequential execution with the same group-entry gates (Appendix B). SimpleHC uses K=4K=4, where shared memory access reduces full-state reads for gate generation and input aggregation from 8 to 2 and writes from 4 to 1 relative to original execution. Each full-state read/write accesses n​CnC elements per token. Algorithm 1 summarizes the forward execution of one group. Matrix columns use zero-based offsets within the group.

4 Infrastructure Design

To realize the efficiency benefits of the simplified design, we optimize the forward and backward execution of SimpleHC with specialized kernels. At the largest tested width (C=6144C=6144), these kernels reduce the additional end-to-end training time over the vanilla residual baseline from 22.5%22.5\% with PyTorch to 2.4%2.4\% (Figure 3). These kernels are implemented using DeepGEMM (Zhao et al., 2025) and Triton (Tillet et al., 2019).

4.1 Forward Fusion with Shared State Access

Grouped reads. Grouped gate generation and batched base reads implement the read side of shared memory access. For x=vec⁡(XL)∈ℝn​C×1x=\operatorname{vec}(X_{L})\in\mathbb{R}^{nC\times 1} and independent gate projections concatenated into W∈ℝn​C×2​K​nW\in\mathbb{R}^{nC\times 2Kn}, we compute

p=W⊤​x,s=x⊤​x,V=XL⊤​H¯pre.p=W^{\top}x,\qquad s=x^{\top}x,\qquad V=X_{L}^{\top}\bar{H}^{\mathrm{pre}}. (6)

Here p∈ℝ2​K​n×1p\in\mathbb{R}^{2Kn\times 1}, ss is scalar, and V∈ℝC×KV\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times K}. One kernel computes p,sp,s from the same loaded state. Gate normalization uses affine-free RMSNorm, with r=(s/(nC)+ϵ)−1/2r=(s/(nC)+\epsilon)^{-1/2} computed from the input state. For each sublayer jj and gate type t∈{pre,post}t\in\{\mathrm{pre},\mathrm{post}\}, the corresponding projection block pjtp_{j}^{t} gives logits ℓjt=αjt​r​pjt+bjt\ell_{j}^{t}=\alpha_{j}^{t}rp_{j}^{t}+b_{j}^{t}. A second kernel fuses this scaling and bias addition with gate activations, avoiding a normalized-state buffer. At n=K=4n=K=4, one 4​C×324C\times 32 projection supplies four read gates and four write gates. A separate batched-read kernel reuses each loaded state tile for all KK distinct bases, storing them contiguously per sublayer. Gate generation and base aggregation each reduce full-state reads from K​n​CKnC to n​CnC elements per token per group.

Fused corrections and deferred write-back. We implement Equations 4 and 5 without stacked output copies or expanded update buffers. Using precomputed coefficients DD, each correction kernel loads preceding CC-dimensional outputs through separate pointers and fuses weighting, summation, and base addition. At K=4K=4, three correction kernels supply the sequential sublayer inputs; one group-exit kernel then fuses all four output allocations with residual addition. Wide-state update traffic falls from 2​K​n​C2KnC to 2​n​C2nC elements per token per group.

4.2 Backward Reuse and Efficient Reductions

We tailor backward kernels to two distinct workloads: wide activation gradients benefit from cross-sublayer reuse, whereas small gate gradients require efficient channel reductions.

For loss ℒ\mathcal{L}, let G=∇Vℒ∈ℝC×KG=\nabla_{V}\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times K}, O=[oL,…,oL+K−1]∈ℝC×KO=[o_{L},\ldots,o_{L+K-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times K}, and E=∇XL+Kℒ∈ℝn×CE=\nabla_{X_{L+K}}\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times C}. These equations give gradient contributions from the base reads and final write-back, with +⁣=\mathrel{+}= denoting accumulation.

Shared activation-gradient access. We compute activation-gradient contributions jointly across the group:

∇XLℒ+=E+H¯preG⊤,∇Oℒ+=E⊤H¯post.\nabla_{X_{L}}\mathcal{L}\mathrel{+}=E+\bar{H}^{\mathrm{pre}}G^{\top},\qquad\nabla_{O}\mathcal{L}\mathrel{+}=E^{\top}\bar{H}^{\mathrm{post}}. (7)

The read backward fuses all KK contributions with the identity gradient EE, avoiding KK expanded gradients and merging. Reusing one scan of EE for all KK output gradients reduces its logical reads from K​n​CKnC to n​CnC elements per token per group (4×4\times at K=4K=4). We fuse projection input gradients with RMS differentiation, avoiding a wide intermediate and a separate normalization-backward pass; weight gradients use a separate GEMM.

Token-packed gate gradients. Gate gradients instead require reductions over the channel dimension:

∇H¯preℒ+=XLG,∇H¯postℒ+=EO.\nabla_{\bar{H}^{\mathrm{pre}}}\mathcal{L}\mathrel{+}=X_{L}G,\qquad\nabla_{\bar{H}^{\mathrm{post}}}\mathcal{L}\mathrel{+}=EO. (8)

At n=K=4n=K=4, each product reduces CC channels to just 16 coefficients per token. We pack four tokens into a 16×1616\times 16 Tensor Core product, accumulate over channels on-chip, and store only the four same-token 4×44\times 4 blocks, eliminating the partial-gradient scratch buffer and extra reduction launch of the channel-tiled fallback for each product.

4.3 Memory-Access and Storage Accounting

The accounting in Table 1 covers logical forward activation reads and writes per token per sublayer, excluding parameters, small coefficient buffers, and attention/FFN internals. Naive mHC materializes mixed states and expanded updates separately; fused mHC combines residual mixing, output allocation, and residual addition.

At group offset a>0a>0, each correction reads one base and aa preceding outputs, then writes one input, costing (a+2)​C(a+2)C elements. Offset a=0a=0 uses its base directly. Averaging over KK sublayers gives

Qcorr​(K)=CK​∑a=1K−1(a+2)=C​(K−1)​(K+4)2​K,Qcorr​(4)=3​C.Q_{\mathrm{corr}}(K)=\frac{C}{K}\sum_{a=1}^{K-1}(a+2)=\frac{C(K-1)(K+4)}{2K},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{corr}}(4)=3C. (9)

Grouped gate generation and base reads each access n​CnC elements per group; final write-back reads and writes the wide state once, adding 2​n​C2nC. Together these contribute 4​n​C/K4nC/K per sublayer. Base writes and output reads for final write-back add 2​C2C, yielding

QSimpleHC​(K)=4​n​CK+2​C+Qcorr​(K).Q_{\mathrm{SimpleHC}}(K)=\frac{4nC}{K}+2C+Q_{\mathrm{corr}}(K). (10)

At n=4n=4, this gives 11.5​C11.5C, 9​C9C, 9.25​C9.25C, and 12.375​C12.375C for K=2,4,8,16K=2,4,8,16, respectively. Thus, K=4K=4 has the lowest logical traffic among these group sizes, rather than over all positive integers. Correction costs grow with KK, offsetting the reduced wide-state traffic at larger group sizes. Our choice of K=4K=4 halves the 18​C18C traffic of fused mHC and identityHC. Removing mixing alone does not reduce these accesses: fused mHC already combines mixing and output allocation in one write-back. The reduction comes from sharing state access across sublayers. Without recomputation, saving one group-entry residual state instead of KK sublayer-entry states reduces the storage of these residual states by 1−1/K1-1/K (75%75\% at K=4K=4).

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

Training setup. We conduct experiments on a MoE model with 15B total and 1B activated parameters (15B-A1B), and evaluate scalability on a 30B-A2B model. Following dots3-note Preview (Dots Studio, 2026), we use MoE backbones (Dai et al., 2024) with MLA (Liu et al., 2024a), alternating one full-attention layer with three sliding-window layers. We train with a sequence length of 8192 using Muon (Liu et al., 2025) on a high-quality mixture of English and Chinese text, code, and mathematics. Unless specified, we use n=4n=4 streams and groups of K=4K=4 sublayers. Appendix A.1 details configurations.

Evaluation. We evaluate knowledge, reasoning, math, code, and Chinese on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and C3 (Sun et al., 2020) for the 15B-A1B studies (Tables 2 and 3). For 30B-A2B (Table 4), we add MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), MMLU-Redux (Gema et al., 2025), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), CMMLU (Li et al., 2024), and CEval (Huang et al., 2023), yielding fourteen benchmarks. Appendix A.3 details few-shot settings and loss reporting for both the 15B-A1B and 30B-A2B models.

5.2 Understanding the Hyper-Connections Architecture

We examine the roles and interactions of read/write gates and residual mixing in the HC architecture (Table 2). HC and mHC share these components but differ in gate conditioning, parameterization, and mixing constraints. Except for HC variants, gates follow the parameterization in Section 3.1.

Configurations. HC w/o mixing retains the HC parameterization but sets Hres=IH^{\mathrm{res}}=I; identityHC makes the same replacement in mHC. mHC w/o Sinkhorn and the unconstrained fixed-gate control use Hres=I+reshape⁡(ℓres)H^{\mathrm{res}}=I+\operatorname{reshape}(\ell^{\mathrm{res}}), without exponentiation or Sinkhorn normalization. Restricted read/write replaces only the indicated gate’s input with the corresponding stream, using per-stream RMS normalization and a C×1C\times 1 projection shared across streams; the other gate retains joint-state conditioning. Fixed read/write sets the indicated gate to 𝟏/n\mathbf{1}/n or 𝟏\mathbf{1}, respectively, while retaining the other components specified in the table.

We observe: (i) Unconstrained mixing is effective, but Sinkhorn diminishes its gains. Retaining unconstrained mixing improves the average score in HC (rows 3 vs. 2). Under the mHC parameterization, unconstrained mixing achieves 56.2, versus 55.0 with Sinkhorn constraints and 55.4 with identity transitions (rows 4–6). Sinkhorn limits the benefit of mixing, leaving performance close to identityHC. (ii) Three components form two effective groups: read/write gating and unconstrained mixing. Without mixing, jointly learned read/write gates achieve an average score of 55.4; fixing either gate lowers it significantly, supporting their treatment as one group. Unconstrained mixing forms the other: with both gates fixed, it achieves 56.0 (row 12). Either group alone is comparable to mHC; combining them improves the score (row 4). (iii) Full-state conditioning improves model quality. With full-state inputs, loss is 1.660. Restricting read/write gates to stream-local inputs raises loss by 0.001/0.003 (rows 6–8), suggesting slightly greater sensitivity in write gates. Section 6.1 analyzes these findings and their implications for SimpleHC.

5.3 Shared Memory Access with Layer-Specific Gating

Table 3 ablates group size, gate reuse, and scalar corrections, with identityHC and mHC as references.

Configurations. Share KK generates gates for KK consecutive sublayers from one group-entry state; K=4K=4 spans two Transformer blocks. Independent gates retain separate parameters for each sublayer, whereas reused gates share one read/write pair across the group. The w/o corrections variant uses only base reads for sublayer inputs without accounting for preceding sublayer output contributions, but retains all sublayer outputs in the group-boundary write-back. All sharing variants use identity residual transitions.

The results highlight three findings: (i) Moderate state sharing preserves model quality. K=2,4K=2,4 match the loss of identityHC, while K=8K=8 slightly increases it (rows 3–6). At K=4K=4, the average score of 55.0 is comparable to mHC and identityHC. We choose K=4K=4 for its competitive quality and lowest memory traffic (Section 4.3). (ii) Layer-specific gates improve quality under shared inputs. At K=4K=4, reusing one read/write gate pair lowers the average score from 55.0 to 53.5 (rows 5 vs. 7). This supports retaining layer-specific gate parameters. (iii) Scalar corrections are important for model performance. Removing corrections raises loss from 1.660 to 1.705 despite retaining all outputs in the final write-back (rows 5 vs. 8). Thus, later sublayers must incorporate preceding outputs even when gate inputs are shared. Section 6.2 analyzes these findings.

5.4 Evaluating SimpleHC at Larger Scale

On the larger 30B-A2B model, SimpleHC matches mHC performance while simplifying both the residual structure and execution. As shown in Table 4, it achieves the same loss of 1.561 as mHC and identityHC and an average benchmark score of 63.1 versus 62.9 for mHC and 62.8 for identityHC. It achieves higher scores on MMLU, MATH, and C3, although it trails mHC on GSM8K and both methods on HumanEval. These results support the scalability of SimpleHC.

5.5 Translating Simplicity into Training Efficiency

We compare end-to-end training overhead against the baseline across scales from C=1024C=1024 to C=6144C=6144 (matching frontier models (Xu et al., 2026; Tencent Hy Team, 2026)). Details are provided in Appendix A.2.

With the efficient implementations, SimpleHC achieves the lowest overhead across all tested scales (Figure 3(a)). At the smallest scale, overhead is 6.3%, versus 26.8% for mHC and 10.1% for identityHC. Despite matching forward activation traffic, mHC incurs additional mixing and Sinkhorn costs, explaining its larger gap from identityHC at smaller scales. Relative overhead generally decreases with width: HC operations scale linearly at fixed nn, whereas expert projections scale quadratically when expert width grows proportionally. At the largest tested scale, SimpleHC cuts overhead from approximately 7.0% for both baselines to 2.4%, eliminating about two-thirds.

We additionally compare against xHC, a promising approach to scaling residual-stream capacity (Zhang et al., 2026). At C=6144C=6144, its training overhead is 27.7%, compared with approximately 7.0% for mHC and 2.4% for SimpleHC (Figure 4). These results position SimpleHC as one of the most efficient HC variants evaluated for scaling foundation models.

Specialized kernels require substantial engineering effort, limiting wider adoption. Thus we also evaluate PyTorch versions (Figure 3(b)), where SimpleHC has the lowest overhead across all tested scales.

Saved activation memory. By reusing group-entry states, SimpleHC reduces estimated storage retained for backward at sublayer boundaries and within HC connections by approximately 31% relative to mHC (Figure 1(b)). Appendix A.2 details the accounting.

6 Analysis

We analyze the design and training stability of SimpleHC. Three conclusions emerge: (i) learned read/write gating provides a minimal effective residual structure; (ii) gating decisions vary across sublayers yet remain predictable from a shared group-entry state; (iii) SimpleHC remains stable under stress and exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training.

6.1 A Minimal Structure for Hyper-Connections

To combine architectural simplicity, competitive performance, and robust scaling, we select learned read/write gating without mixing as a minimal effective residual structure for Hyper-Connections. This avoids the propagation risks of cumulative residual mixing, as analyzed below.

Learned read/write gating and unconstrained mixing form two effective groups: each achieves performance comparable to mHC, with further gains when combined (Table 2). Appendix C compares their weighting mechanisms. However, unconstrained mixing repeatedly transforms earlier contributions through residual matrix products, risking cumulative amplification and training instability (Xie et al., 2025). We observe unconstrained mixing with fixed gates produces larger peak residual-path coefficients than identityHC, consistent with these amplification risks (Figure 7, Appendix D.1).

Sinkhorn constraints mitigate these risks (Xie et al., 2025), but constrained mixing adds little benefit over learned read/write gating alone. We therefore retain learned gates without mixing and use full-state inputs for better loss and benchmark scores (Table 2). Full-state and stream-local conditioning incur the same residual-state input traffic, as both read all streams.

6.2 Why Shared Memory Access Is Effective

We examine why shared memory access benefits from layer-specific gates and remains effective with shared inputs through gate variation and predictability analyses.

Gate variation across sublayers. Read and write gates exhibit distinct allocation patterns across sublayers of the 15B identityHC model (Figures 8(a) and 5(a)). These differences motivate retaining layer-specific gates under shared inputs, consistent with their advantage over gate reuse (Table 3).

Predictability from the group-entry state. We examine whether subsequent gates are predictable from the group-entry state to assess the feasibility of sharing gate inputs. We train layer-specific predictors to recover subsequent read/write gates of a frozen 15B identityHC model from the group-entry state. The predictors use the SimpleHC parameterization and are initialized from the corresponding teacher gate parameters. Only predictors are trained. The “Frozen teacher gates” baseline uses these mappings without training. In Figure 5(b), it predicts write gates more accurately than uniform random gates (MAE 0.0504 vs. 0.4086), indicating predictive ability from earlier inputs even without adaptation. Training further reduces MAE to 0.0103, suggesting that layer-specific mappings closely approximate subsequent gates from shared inputs and supporting the shared memory access design. Read gates show the same trend (Figure 8(b)). Appendix D.3 details the protocol.

Sharing gate inputs does not remove the need for sequential output contributions: removing scalar corrections raises loss from 1.660 to 1.705 despite retaining the final write-back.

6.3 Does Simplification Compromise Training Stability?

Training stability is essential for reliable scaling, as instabilities absent in smaller models can emerge at larger scales (Wortsman et al., 2024). We examine whether the simplifications in SimpleHC compromise training stability. During 15B training, SimpleHC shows smaller gradient-norm fluctuations and lower rolling standard deviation than mHC and identityHC early after warmup (Figure 6(a)); all three reach comparable ranges later. Shared-input gating may reduce sensitivity to within-group state fluctuations by conditioning decisions on an earlier state, loosely analogous to stabilization through historical averaging. This could contribute to smoother training of SimpleHC.

To emulate large-scale training stability challenges, we stress-test 230B-A6B MoE models at 10×10\times the reference learning rate. In Figure 6(b), mHC exhibits gradient spikes reaching approximately 1.9×1061.9\times 10^{6}, while SimpleHC and identityHC maintain bounded gradient norms. Appendix E details the settings and analyzes potential causes of mHC instability.

7 Related Work

Hyper-Connections and Variants. Hyper-Connections expand the residual pathway into multiple streams with learned read, write, and mixing operations (Zhu et al., 2025). Subsequent work constrains mixing to doubly stochastic matrices (Xie et al., 2025), reduces constraint-enforcement costs (Yang and Gao, 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Dandachi and Diggs-Galligan, 2026), or explores other constraints for stable propagation and stream diversity (Liu et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). Other designs modify read/write structures (Qiu et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026) or use sparse updates to support more streams (Zhang et al., 2026).

Understanding and Simplifying Hyper-Connections. Recent analyses reveal uneven stream utilization, redundancy, and concentrated read/write routing in HC models (Peng et al., 2026; Alimaskina et al., 2026). Prior work also reports that removing residual mixing can largely preserve model quality (Guo et al., 2026), with related evidence from finetuning (Oldenburg et al., 2026). These observations motivate examining which interactions account for the benefits. Our study identifies learned read/write gating and unconstrained mixing as two independently effective groups, while showing that Sinkhorn constraints diminish the gains from mixing. These findings explain why learned gating alone remains competitive with mHC (Xie et al., 2025) and motivate an additive structure whose execution we further simplify through shared memory access.

Efficient Execution of Residual Aggregation. Richer residual pathways introduce storage and data-movement costs beyond their arithmetic overhead. Prior work reduces these costs through block-wise aggregation and staged computation (Team et al., 2026), kernel fusion and recomputation (Xie et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026), and optimized multi-stream execution (Zhang et al., 2026). SimpleHC further reduces repeated residual-state access across sublayers by sharing gate inputs while retaining layer-specific parameters. Together with the additive residual structure, this permits consolidated reads and deferred writes, with scalar corrections preserving sequential output contributions for the chosen gates.

8 Conclusion

In this work, we study how the components of the Hyper-Connections architecture contribute to model performance and training cost. Our study identifies learned read/write gating as a minimal effective structure, while unconstrained mixing offers gains with propagation risks. Beyond removing mixing, we introduce shared memory access to reduce repeated residual-state accesses, with gate analyses supporting layer-specific mappings conditioned on shared inputs. Together, they form SimpleHC, simplifying residual structure and execution. SimpleHC matches mHC performance on 15B and 30B MoE models, reduces additional training overhead from 7.0%7.0\% to 2.4%2.4\% at the largest tested scale, and exhibits smoother gradient dynamics while remaining stable under stress. SimpleHC thus combines architectural simplicity, execution efficiency, training stability, and scalability.

Appendix

Appendix A Experimental Settings

This section provides additional details on the experimental settings. Tables 2 and 3 use the 15B-A1B setup, and Table 4 uses the 30B-A2B setup. Efficiency measurements use the separate configurations in Appendix A.2. Gate-analysis and stability figures are documented in Appendices D and E, respectively.

A.1 Model and Training Configurations

Table 5 reports the backbone architectures and training recipes for the 15B-A1B design-space studies and the 30B-A2B scaling experiments. Parameter counts are rounded; activated counts exclude embedding and output layers. Both backbones apply headwise sigmoid gating to attention outputs before the output projection (Qiu et al., 2026b).

Training hyperparameters. Table 5 summarizes the model configurations and training hyperparameters. Muon updates backbone matrix weights in attention and MLP/MoE modules; AdamW updates embeddings, output weights, normalization parameters, and HC gate parameters. We use a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) (Hu et al., 2024) learning-rate schedule with 1,000 warmup steps, followed by a constant learning rate and arccos decay over the final 20%20\% of training.

For the gate-reuse variant in Table 3, each group uses one learned read/write gate pair instead of four layer-specific pairs. The gates are computed from the group-entry state and reused across all sublayers.

Initialization. We follow the initialization scheme of the mHC implementation in the xHC repository.11 1 https://github.com/aHapBean/xHC For identityHC and SimpleHC, we use an analogous initialization scheme for the read/write gate parameters, with residual transitions fixed to the identity.

A.2 Efficiency Benchmark Settings

We evaluate training efficiency across model scales by varying hidden width from 1024 to 6144, as summarized in Table 6. To limit memory requirements and avoid introducing parallelism changes, all benchmark models use eight Transformer layers. This allows comparisons across widths without the resource demands of full-depth models. At each width, residual variants share the backbone, batch sizes, and parallel configuration. Since both residual operations and backbone computation repeat across layers, these measurements provide a representative estimate of relative training overhead in deeper models with the same parallel configuration.

All models use MLA with one full-attention layer followed by three sliding-window layers of window size 512. The first layer has a dense FFN; the remaining seven use 256 routed experts with top-8 routing and one shared expert. We use BF16, a sequence length of 8192, and a global batch size of 256. CUDA Graph is enabled for all methods, with activation recomputation disabled. mHC, identityHC, and SimpleHC use four residual streams, and SimpleHC groups four sublayers.

xHC comparisons. We benchmark xHC under the same timing protocol described above (Figure 4). Our efficient xHC implementation is numerically validated against the official implementation.1 xHC uses N=16N=16 residual streams with k=4k=4 active streams.

Saved activation storage accounting. We estimate storage retained for backward after one microbatch forward pass, covering sublayer inputs and outputs, residual states and copies, base reads, HC auxiliary tensors, and the decoder output before final normalization (Table 7). Shared storage is counted once, while distinct copies are counted separately. The accounting excludes attention/FFN internals, LM-head/loss buffers, model and optimizer states, temporary workspaces, and allocator/CUDA Graph reservations. These source-level estimates are not total activation or peak device memory. Figure 1(b) uses microbatch size one; both estimates scale linearly with microbatch size, leaving the relative reduction unchanged.

The models use eight layers (16 sublayers), n=4n=4, and no recomputation; SimpleHC uses four groups with K=4K=4. For TT local microbatch tokens, let U=2​T​CU=2TC bytes denote one BF16 narrow activation. The mHC residual inputs occupy U+15×4​U=61​UU+15\times 4U=61U: the first uses a broadcast view of the dense input, followed by 15 wide inputs. SimpleHC retains two wide copies for gate projection and base reads in the first group, and one per later group, totaling 8​U+3×4​U=20​U8U+3\times 4U=20U. Each group jointly allocates four base reads; the first sublayer input keeps the entire allocation live through a view. Beyond that input, already counted in the input row, the remaining slices contribute 3​U3U per group, or 12​U12U overall. identityHC has a similar saved-storage footprint to mHC, as both retain wide residual states at each sublayer.

HC auxiliary tensors are FP32 and include projections, gates, inverse-RMS statistics, and mixing or correction intermediates. The mHC path retains 73 elements per token per sublayer (4672​T4672T bytes overall); SimpleHC retains 103 per token per group (1648​T1648T bytes), including contiguous gate copies and correction coefficients. At C=2048C=2048 and T=8192T=8192, total storage falls from 3044.5 to 2092.875 MiB, a 31.26%31.26\% reduction. Across the six evaluated widths, reductions range from 31.0%31.0\% to 31.7%31.7\%, supporting the rounded 31%31\% summary.

A.3 Evaluation Protocols

We report validation loss on the Pile test split (Gao et al., 2020) in Tables 2, 3, and 4.

For the 15B-A1B component studies, we evaluate MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) in a 5-shot setting, HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) in a 10-shot setting, MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) in a 4-shot setting, and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) and C3 (Sun et al., 2020), both in a 3-shot setting. For the 30B-A2B evaluation, we retain these settings and add MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), MMLU-Redux (Gema et al., 2025), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), CMMLU (Li et al., 2024), and CEval (Huang et al., 2023) with 5-shot evaluation; BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023) and DROP (Dua et al., 2019) with 3-shot evaluation; GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) with 4-shot evaluation; and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) with zero-shot evaluation.

Appendix B Exact Reconstruction with Scalar Corrections

We analyze the forward execution in Algorithm 1.

We prove that scalar reconstruction and deferred write-back are equivalent to sequential execution with the same shared-input gates. Both executions use Equation 3, identical parameters, and identical random choices for any stochastic operations. Define the sequential reference by X~L=XL\widetilde{X}_{L}=X_{L} and

u~j=X~j⊤​h¯jpre,o~j=Fj​(u~j),X~j+1=X~j+h¯jpost​o~j⊤.\widetilde{u}_{j}=\widetilde{X}_{j}^{\top}\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}},\qquad\widetilde{o}_{j}=F_{j}(\widetilde{u}_{j}),\qquad\widetilde{X}_{j+1}=\widetilde{X}_{j}+\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{post}}\widetilde{o}_{j}^{\top}. (11)

Forward equivalence. At j=Lj=L, Equation 4 has no correction terms, so uL=u~Lu_{L}=\widetilde{u}_{L} and oL=o~Lo_{L}=\widetilde{o}_{L}. Assume ok=o~ko_{k}=\widetilde{o}_{k} for L≤k<jL\leq k<j. Expanding the reference updates and applying the read decomposition in Equation 2 gives

u~j=XL⊤​h¯jpre+∑k=Lj−1((h¯jpre)⊤​h¯kpost)​o~k=uj.\widetilde{u}_{j}=X_{L}^{\top}\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}+\sum_{k=L}^{j-1}\bigl((\bar{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}})^{\top}\bar{h}_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}\bigr)\widetilde{o}_{k}=u_{j}. (12)

Thus o~j=oj\widetilde{o}_{j}=o_{j}, completing the induction. Summing the reference updates also yields exactly the group-boundary state in Equation 5.

Gradient equivalence. The two executions define the same function of XLX_{L} and the parameters, so their derivatives agree wherever this function is differentiable. Gradients must include the dependence of every gate on XLX_{L}; detaching gates would invalidate this equivalence. Nondifferentiable operations require consistent derivative conventions. The equivalence holds in exact arithmetic; floating-point results may differ with reduction order and precision. It does not assert equivalence to gates conditioned on each updated sublayer state.

Appendix C Read/Write Gating and Unconstrained Mixing

We examine the weighting mechanisms of the two interaction groups in Table 2 to interpret their comparable empirical performance. Both control how earlier outputs contribute to later inputs, but place learnable flexibility at different points along the residual path. For a fixed token, the residual-path coefficient carrying output oko_{k} into a later input uju_{j} is

cj,k=(hjpre)⊤Φk+1→jhkpost,Φk+1→j=Hj−1res⋯Hk+1res,c_{j,k}=(h_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}})^{\top}\Phi_{k+1\to j}h_{k}^{\mathrm{post}},\qquad\Phi_{k+1\to j}=H_{j-1}^{\mathrm{res}}\cdots H_{k+1}^{\mathrm{res}}, (13)

where an empty product is II. With learned read/write gates and identity transitions, this reduces to

cj,k=(hjpre)⊤​hkpost.c_{j,k}=(h_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}})^{\top}h_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}. (14)

For unconstrained mixing with the fixed gates used in our comparisons, hjpre=𝟏/nh_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}=\mathbf{1}/n and hkpost=𝟏h_{k}^{\mathrm{post}}=\mathbf{1}, the same coefficient becomes

cj,k=1n​𝟏⊤​Φk+1→j​𝟏.c_{j,k}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\Phi_{k+1\to j}\mathbf{1}. (15)

Learned read/write gates jointly determine historical-output weights: the write gate controls how an output is allocated across streams, while a later read gate determines how that allocation contributes to its input. Unconstrained mixing instead modifies the allocation through intervening residual transitions, even with fixed read/write gates.

Under the mHC gate parameterization, read and write gates lie in (0,1)(0,1) and (0,2)(0,2), respectively, bounding their inner-product coefficients between 00 and 2​n2n. Unconstrained mixing permits signed coefficients without a comparable parameter-independent bound. It therefore offers additional weighting freedom, but also introduces the propagation risks discussed in the main text.

These mechanisms provide alternative ways to learn effective historical-output weights, offering a structural explanation for why either group can achieve competitive performance. Learning both groups combines these controls, consistent with the further gains in Table 2. Their comparable scores remain an empirical finding rather than a consequence of equivalent expressivity.

Appendix D Gate Analysis Details

This section details the measurements and experimental protocols for the analyses in Sections 6.1 and 6.2.

D.1 Residual-Path Contribution Coefficients

Figure 7 compares the final checkpoints of two 15B-A1B models: unconstrained mixing with fixed read/write gates and learned read/write gates with identity transitions. Both have 24 Transformer blocks, 48 sublayers, and four residual streams (Table 2, rows 12 and 6). We use 1,024 analysis sequences and sample 256 non-special-token positions per sequence with a fixed seed. Both models use the same 262,144 token occurrences. Sublayer indices alternate attention and FFN, from 0 to 47.

For each source aa and later target bb, we evaluate the coefficient cb,ac_{b,a} in Equation 13 and plot Mb,a=maxt∈𝒯⁡|cb,a​(t)|M_{b,a}=\max_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|c_{b,a}(t)|. The mixing configuration fixes hpre=𝟏/4h^{\mathrm{pre}}=\mathbf{1}/4 and hpost=𝟏h^{\mathrm{post}}=\mathbf{1}; the identity configuration uses learned gates. These coefficients use raw write gates, without division by two. Each cell may attain its maximum at a different token. These sampled residual-path coefficients are neither matrix norms nor full-network Jacobians and do not alone establish training instability or increasing amplification with propagation distance.

D.2 Gate Variation Across Sublayers

We use the same identityHC checkpoint and sampled token occurrences. For sublayers a,ba,b, the plotted difference is

Ds​(a,b)=14​|𝒯|​∑t∈𝒯∑i=14|qa,is​(t)−qb,is​(t)|,qpre=hpre,qpost=hpost/2.D^{s}(a,b)=\frac{1}{4|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{4}\left|q_{a,i}^{s}(t)-q_{b,i}^{s}(t)\right|,\qquad q^{\mathrm{pre}}=h^{\mathrm{pre}},\quad q^{\mathrm{post}}=h^{\mathrm{post}}/2. (16)

Absolute differences are computed for matched token positions and stream indices before averaging. Figure 5(a) shows write gates; Figure 8(a) shows read gates. Both use a power-normalized color scale with γ=0.4\gamma=0.4 over [0,1][0,1]; colorbar labels give actual MAE. The matrices are symmetric with zero diagonals and measure gate variation rather than causal propagation.

D.3 Prediction from the Group-Entry State

The prediction experiment freezes the final identityHC checkpoint and groups its 48 sublayers into 12 groups of K=4K=4. The teacher always executes with its own gates. Predictors receive only the same-token group-entry state XLX_{L}; their outputs never alter the teacher trajectory.

Predictors and targets. For L≤j<L+KL\leq j<L+K and s∈{pre,post}s\in\{\mathrm{pre},\mathrm{post}\}, the target is hjs=gjs​(Xj)h_{j}^{s}=g_{j}^{s}(X_{j}) from the frozen teacher. Each predictor uses the SimpleHC gate parameterization with independent parameters for every sublayer and gate type:

zL\displaystyle z_{L} =RMSNorm⁡(vec⁡(XL)),\displaystyle=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\operatorname{vec}(X_{L})), (17)
ℓ^js\displaystyle\widehat{\ell}_{j}^{s} =α^js​(W^js)⊤​zL+b^js,\displaystyle=\widehat{\alpha}_{j}^{s}(\widehat{W}_{j}^{s})^{\top}z_{L}+\widehat{b}_{j}^{s},
h^jpre\displaystyle\widehat{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}} =σ(ℓ^jpre),h^jpost=2σ(ℓ^jpost).\displaystyle=\sigma(\widehat{\ell}_{j}^{\mathrm{pre}}),\qquad\widehat{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{post}}=2\sigma(\widehat{\ell}_{j}^{\mathrm{post}}).

The input dimension is 4×1792=71684\times 1792=7168, with 32 gate values per group and approximately 2.75M trainable parameters in total. Projections, scales, and biases are initialized from the corresponding teacher parameters. Read and write gates are trained jointly; teacher states and targets are detached.

Training and evaluation. We train the predictor for 10,000 steps with MSE loss, a global batch size of 64, and a sequence length of 8,192. We use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) with β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, zero weight decay, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The learning rate increases linearly from zero to 10−310^{-3} over 500 warmup steps, then follows cosine decay to 10−510^{-5}. Validation uses a fixed set of 2,048 sequences, excluding special tokens. We evaluate every 200 steps and use the final step-10,000 checkpoint for testing, without dev-based checkpoint selection.

Baselines and metrics. The frozen reference applies each sublayer mapping copied from the teacher to the shared entry state without adaptation. It remains input-dependent and does not reuse one gate pair across sublayers. In the plots, this reference is labeled “Frozen teacher gates.” The random baseline samples independent hpre∼𝒰⁡(0,1)h^{\mathrm{pre}}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) and hpost∼𝒰⁡(0,2)h^{\mathrm{post}}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,2) for each token, sublayer, and stream. The constant baseline uses mean gates fitted on training data. MAE is computed by averaging absolute errors over valid tokens, groups, future offsets 1–3, and streams; write gates are divided by two. Offset 0 is excluded.

Experimental results. On 102,400 test sequences, the final predictor achieves read/write MAE of 0.01653/0.01034, compared with 0.05817/0.05044 for frozen mappings and 0.07345/0.06893 for constant mean gates. Together with the improvements over uniform random gates on the dev set, these results support closely approximating subsequent gates from shared entry states using layer-specific mappings.

Appendix E Training Stability Details

This section details the stress-test design, training dynamics, and instability diagnostics supporting Section 6.3.

E.1 Stress-Test Design and Settings

To emulate stability challenges in large-scale training, we combine 64 layers, 512 routed experts with top-8 routing, and a learning rate 10×10\times the reference value. This stresses optimization through a longer propagation path, higher sparsity, and larger updates. A hidden width of 2816 keeps activated parameters near 6B, yielding a 230B-A6B model. The experiment tests robustness under these combined pressures rather than isolating individual factors.

All variants use the backbone in Table 8. MLA alternates full and sliding-window attention in a 1:3 pattern, with 72 heads and window size 512. The first FFN is dense with width 7936; the remaining 63 use experts of width 832 and one shared expert. Training uses BF16, microbatch size 1, and Muon with momentum 0.95, weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The WSD schedule uses 4,000 linear warmup steps, followed by the peak learning rate throughout the comparison window. HC variants use n=4n=4; mHC uses 20 Sinkhorn iterations, and SimpleHC uses K=4K=4.

E.2 Training Dynamics

Standard training. During 15B training, SimpleHC shows smaller gradient-norm fluctuations early after warmup than mHC and identityHC, with comparable ranges later (Figure 6(a)). The maximum 1,000-step rolling standard deviation after warmup is 0.032 for SimpleHC, versus 0.206 for mHC and 0.248 for identityHC, indicating smoother standard training.

Stress testing. Under stress, mHC exhibits gradient spikes reaching approximately 1.9×1061.9\times 10^{6}, whereas SimpleHC and identityHC remain bounded (Figure 6(b)). These spikes in mHC are accompanied by loss spikes (Figure 9) and growing branch-output scales, especially in the FFN. SimpleHC and identityHC show no comparable sustained growth (Figure 10), supporting stable training despite the structural and execution simplifications.

E.3 Analysis of Stress-Test Results

SimpleHC and identityHC maintain stable optimization under the combined stress setting, indicating that removing residual mixing, with or without shared gate inputs, can preserve training stability. SimpleHC remains comparable to identityHC despite sharing gate inputs across sublayers. In contrast, mHC exhibits instability in both forward activations and backward gradients. To investigate this behavior, we inspect its branch outputs, residual mixing matrices, and gradient paths.

In a captured early-layer MoE event, an input RMS of 0.294 produced a branch-output RMS of 2.31×1042.31\times 10^{4} before write gating, locating the initial large values in the FFN rather than residual mixing at this sublayer. In the observed stress setting, 20 Sinkhorn iterations did not always suffice to produce a doubly stochastic matrix. In one captured case, row sums remained (2,1,0.5,0.5)(2,1,0.5,0.5), increasing same-token RMS from 5.42×1045.42\times 10^{4} to 7.50×1047.50\times 10^{4}. Mixing could therefore further amplify existing FFN outliers. These observations also suggest a possible rationale for the SwiGLU clamping used in DeepSeek-V4 (Xu et al., 2026): limiting FFN outliers before they enter the residual pathway. Residual mixing also introduces an additional gradient path because HresH^{\mathrm{res}} depends on the input. For Y=Hres​(X)​XY=H^{\mathrm{res}}(X)X, the differential is d​Y=Hres​d​X+(d​Hres)​X\mathrm{d}Y=H^{\mathrm{res}}\mathrm{d}X+(\mathrm{d}H^{\mathrm{res}})X: the first term propagates through the fixed matrix, while the second captures changes in the mixing matrix itself. In one captured backward spike, the gate-input gradient norm was approximately 9.4×9.4\times that of the fixed-matrix path in the same call. Bounds computed from the recorded read/write gates and upstream gradients made their contributions negligible, implicating the dynamic mixing path. Whether this anomaly reflects mathematical sensitivity or numerical effects in backward remains unresolved. Identity transitions set d​Hres=0\mathrm{d}H^{\mathrm{res}}=0, eliminating this additional path, consistent with the stable training observed in identityHC and SimpleHC.
